_meta.label: Outside reading — not part of the curriculum
_meta.notice: These are independent research sources chosen by Weekly for the counselor's own intellectual growth. They are NOT part of the CBI-SUA (University of Cincinnati) or Living in Balance (Hazelden) materials, are not endorsed by them, and should not be presented to group members as program content. Some support the lesson's approach, some question or complicate it.
_meta.verification: Every DOI was confirmed as registered in Crossref with matching title/authors/venue and its abstract read via OpenAlex or Semantic Scholar; every non-DOI URL was fetched live on 2026-11-04. Takeaways are paraphrased, not quoted.

stances.questions: critique, limits, mixed evidence, or an alternative view
stances.context: background that frames the lesson without taking a side

cbi-pre-1.title: TIP 35: Enhancing Motivation for Change in Substance Use Disorder Treatment
cbi-pre-1.authors: Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration
cbi-pre-1.takeaway: SAMHSA's motivation guideline treats resistance as a normal, changeable state rather than a fixed trait, which is the stance behind naming barriers to treatment without arguing about them.

cbi-pre-1.title: Principles of Drug Abuse Treatment for Criminal Justice Populations: A Research-Based Guide
cbi-pre-1.takeaway: NIDA's criminal-justice guide argues that treatment does not have to be voluntary to work, so members who are only in group because a court or parole sent them can still benefit.

cbi-pre-1.title: The Use of Legal Coercion in the Treatment of Substance Abusers: An Overview and Critical Analysis of Thirty Years of Research
cbi-pre-1.authors: Stefanie Klag, Frances O’Callaghan, Peter A. Creed
cbi-pre-1.takeaway: A critical review of 30 years of coercion research says the evidence that legally pressured treatment works is weaker and more mixed than often claimed, partly because 'mandated' and 'feeling coerced' are not the same thing.

cbi-pre-1.title: The effectiveness of compulsory drug treatment: A systematic review
cbi-pre-1.authors: Dan Werb, Adeeba Kamarulzaman, Meredith C. Meacham, et al.
cbi-pre-1.takeaway: This systematic review found little evidence that compulsory drug treatment improves outcomes and some signs of harm; it mostly covers locked compulsory centres, but it is a reminder that pressure alone is not the active ingredient.

cbi-pre-2.title: A Meta-Analysis of Motivational Interviewing: Twenty-Five Years of Empirical Studies
cbi-pre-2.authors: Brad Lundahl, Chelsea Kunz, Cynthia Brownell, et al.
cbi-pre-2.takeaway: Across 25 years of trials, motivational interviewing gave small but reliable gains over no treatment, which backs the session's move of letting members voice their own reasons to change.

cbi-pre-2.title: Mechanisms of change in motivational interviewing: a review and preliminary evaluation of the evidence
cbi-pre-2.takeaway: Clients' own change talk and their sense of a gap between use and what they want were among the most consistent predictors of better outcomes in MI research.

cbi-pre-2.title: Motivational interviewing for substance abuse
cbi-pre-2.authors: Geir Smedslund, Rigmor C. Berg, Karianne Thune Hammerstrøm, et al.
cbi-pre-2.takeaway: The Cochrane review found MI beats no intervention, but rated most of the evidence low quality and found little advantage over other active treatments.

cbi-pre-2.title: Motivational Interviewing
cbi-pre-2.authors: Jennifer E. Hettema, Julie Steele, William R. Miller
cbi-pre-2.takeaway: This review found MI's effects vary a lot across counselors and settings and were larger when it was not delivered from a manual, a caution for scripted group versions.

cbi-pre-3.title: Mechanisms of change in motivational interviewing: a review and preliminary evaluation of the evidence
cbi-pre-3.takeaway: In this review of MI mechanisms, using a decisional-balance exercise was among the techniques most strongly linked to better outcomes.

cbi-pre-3.title: Motivational Interviewing and Decisional Balance: Contrasting Responses to Client Ambivalence
cbi-pre-3.authors: William R. Miller, Gary S. Rose
cbi-pre-3.takeaway: Miller and Rose argue that a full pros-and-cons list can keep an ambivalent person stuck, or even talk them out of change, and that evoking reasons for change is the better tool when the goal is change.

cbi-pre-3.title: TIP 35: Enhancing Motivation for Change in Substance Use Disorder Treatment
cbi-pre-3.authors: Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration
cbi-pre-3.takeaway: SAMHSA's guideline treats weighing pros and cons as one way to tip a person's balance toward change, used alongside empathic listening rather than as a stand-alone worksheet.

cbi-pre-3.title: Motivational interviewing with offenders: A systematic review
cbi-pre-3.takeaway: McMurran's review of MI with offenders found mixed results and called for more research on whether it improves retention, readiness, and reconviction.

cbi-1.title: The positive effects of cognitive–behavioral programs for offenders: A meta-analysis of factors associated with effective treatment
cbi-1.authors: Nana A. Landenberger, Mark W. Lipsey
cbi-1.takeaway: This meta-analysis found that cognitive-behavioral programs for offenders cut reoffending substantially, with the biggest effects for higher-risk people and well-implemented programs, the same model CBI-SUA builds on.

cbi-1.title: Effects of Cognitive-Behavioral Programs for Criminal Offenders
cbi-1.authors: Mark W. Lipsey, Nana A. Landenberger, Sandra Jo Wilson
cbi-1.venue: Campbell Systematic Reviews: Better Evidence for a Better World
cbi-1.takeaway: The Campbell review found no meaningful difference between brand-name CBT programs; quality of delivery and facilitator training mattered more than which curriculum was used.

cbi-1.title: Stages of change and psychotherapy outcomes: A review and meta‐analysis
cbi-1.authors: Paul M. Krebs, John C. Norcross, Joey Nicholson, et al.
cbi-1.takeaway: Readiness to change predicted therapy outcomes across many studies, which supports rating members' readiness at the start.

cbi-1.title: Time for a change: putting the Transtheoretical (Stages of Change) Model to rest
cbi-1.takeaway: West argues the stages-of-change model is a poor guide for practice because readiness shifts quickly and the stage boundaries are arbitrary; simple questions about wanting to change may work as well.

cbi-2.title: Relaxation training for anxiety: a ten-years systematic review with meta-analysis
cbi-2.authors: Gian Mauro Manzoni, Francesco Pagnini, Gianluca Castelnuovo, et al.
cbi-2.takeaway: A meta-analysis of relaxation training found consistent drops in anxiety, which supports teaching breathing and relaxation as quick tools for tense craving moments.

cbi-2.title: Paradoxical effects of thought suppression
cbi-2.authors: Daniel M. Wegner, David J. Schneider, Samuel Roberts Carter, et al.
cbi-2.venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
cbi-2.takeaway: Wegner's thought-suppression experiments showed that trying not to think about something can backfire, but giving people a specific replacement thought reduced the rebound, which fits planned distraction and self-talk.

cbi-2.title: Surfing the urge: Brief mindfulness-based intervention for college student smokers
cbi-2.takeaway: A brief urge-surfing trial suggests an alternative to distraction: mindfulness did not reduce urges themselves but changed how people responded to them, so accepting an urge may beat fighting it.

cbi-2.title: Paradoxical effects of thought suppression: a meta-analysis of controlled studies
cbi-2.authors: Jonathan S. Abramowitz, David F. Tolin, Gordon P. Street
cbi-2.takeaway: A meta-analysis of controlled studies found that thoughts tend to rebound after people stop suppressing them, though effects varied across studies, so planned distraction works better than simply 'not thinking about it'.

cbi-3.title: An initial meta-analysis of Acceptance and Commitment Therapy for treating substance use disorders
cbi-3.authors: Eric B. Lee, Woolee An, Michael E. Levin, et al.
cbi-3.takeaway: This first meta-analysis of Acceptance and Commitment Therapy for substance use found a small-to-medium advantage over active comparison treatments; ACT relies heavily on clarifying values, as this session does.

cbi-3.title: Motivational Interviewing: Helping People Change and Grow (4th ed.)
cbi-3.takeaway: Miller and Rollnick describe exploring personal values as a way to surface the gap between who a person wants to be and what use is doing, without the counselor pushing.

cbi-3.title: Motivational interviewing for substance abuse
cbi-3.authors: Geir Smedslund, Rigmor C. Berg, Karianne Thune Hammerstrøm, et al.
cbi-3.takeaway: Values work borrows from motivational approaches, and the Cochrane review rates the evidence for MI in substance use as mostly low quality, so expectations for a single values exercise should stay modest.

cbi-4.title: Mechanisms of change in motivational interviewing: a review and preliminary evaluation of the evidence
cbi-4.takeaway: Decisional-balance work was among the specific techniques most linked to better outcomes in this review of MI mechanisms.

cbi-4.title: Motivational Interviewing and Decisional Balance: Contrasting Responses to Client Ambivalence
cbi-4.authors: William R. Miller, Gary S. Rose
cbi-4.takeaway: Miller and Rose caution that a neutral cost-benefit tally can reinforce reasons to keep using; when the aim is change, eliciting the person's own reasons to change is preferred.

cbi-4.title: TIP 35: Enhancing Motivation for Change in Substance Use Disorder Treatment
cbi-4.authors: Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration
cbi-4.takeaway: SAMHSA's TIP places cost-benefit exploration within the contemplation stage and pairs it with reflective listening so the exercise does not become a debate.

cbi-5.title: Building a practically useful theory of goal setting and task motivation: A 35-year odyssey
cbi-5.authors: Edwin A. Locke, Gary P. Latham
cbi-5.takeaway: Thirty-five years of goal-setting research shows that specific, challenging but realistic goals improve performance more than vague 'do your best' goals.

cbi-5.title: Implementation Intentions and Goal Achievement: A Meta‐analysis of Effects and Processes
cbi-5.takeaway: Meta-analysis of implementation intentions found that 'if X happens, I will do Y' plans reliably raise goal follow-through.

cbi-5.title: Goals Gone Wild: The Systematic Side Effects of Overprescribing Goal Setting
cbi-5.authors: Lisa D. Ordóñez, Maurice E. Schweitzer, Adam D. Galinsky, Max H. Bazerman
cbi-5.takeaway: These authors warn that goals that are too narrow or pressured can backfire, narrowing attention and crowding out other priorities, a reason to keep goals realistic and member-owned.

cbi-6.title: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Substance Use Disorders
cbi-6.authors: R. Kathryn McHugh, Bridget A. Hearon, Michael W. Otto
cbi-6.takeaway: A clinical review of CBT for substance use describes the same core idea taught here: thoughts and beliefs shape feelings and behavior, and changing them changes use.

cbi-6.title: Cognitive-Behavioral Treatment With Adult Alcohol and Illicit Drug Users: A Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials
cbi-6.venue: Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs
cbi-6.takeaway: Across 53 controlled trials, CBT produced small but significant improvements in alcohol and drug use.

cbi-6.title: Cognitive–behavioral treatment for alcohol dependence: a review of evidence for its hypothesized mechanisms of action
cbi-6.takeaway: This review found little evidence that CBT works through the mechanisms it claims (better coping skills, changed thinking); it works, but the reasons are not clear.

cbi-6.title: Do we need to challenge thoughts in cognitive behavior therapy?
cbi-6.takeaway: Longmore and Worrell found little evidence that challenging thoughts adds much to the behavioral parts of CBT, which questions the iceberg model's focus on thinking.

cbi-7.title: The positive effects of cognitive–behavioral programs for offenders: A meta-analysis of factors associated with effective treatment
cbi-7.authors: Nana A. Landenberger, Mark W. Lipsey
cbi-7.takeaway: The offender CBT meta-analysis supports teaching people to link situations, thoughts, and consequences, since programs built on this produced large drops in reoffending.

cbi-7.title: A cognitive model of drug urges and drug-use behavior: Role of automatic and nonautomatic processes
cbi-7.takeaway: Tiffany's model argues much drug use runs on automatic habit without a conscious thought-then-choice step, so the behavior chain may describe some lapses better than others.

cbi-7.title: Cognitive-Behavioral Treatment With Adult Alcohol and Illicit Drug Users: A Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials
cbi-7.venue: Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs
cbi-7.takeaway: CBT effects in substance use are real but modest overall, strongest when compared with no treatment.

cbi-8.title: Relapse Prevention for Alcohol and Drug Problems: That Was Zen, This Is Tao
cbi-8.authors: Katie A. Witkiewitz, G. Alan Marlatt
cbi-8.takeaway: Witkiewitz and Marlatt's update of relapse prevention keeps high-risk situations at the center but treats them as interacting with stable background risks, matching the session's split between life history, lifestyle, and triggers.

cbi-8.title: Relapse prevention for addictive behaviors
cbi-8.authors: Christian S. Hendershot, Katie A. Witkiewitz, William H. George, et al.
cbi-8.venue: Substance Abuse Treatment, Prevention, and Policy
cbi-8.takeaway: This review summarizes the evidence that identifying personal high-risk situations is a core and well-supported part of relapse prevention.

cbi-8.title: Rehabilitating criminal justice policy and practice
cbi-8.authors: D. A. Andrews, James L. Bonta
cbi-8.takeaway: The Risk-Need-Responsivity model adds that for justice-involved people, risky situations overlap with criminogenic needs like antisocial peers and attitudes.

cbi-8.title: A cognitive model of drug urges and drug-use behavior: Role of automatic and nonautomatic processes
cbi-8.takeaway: Because use can become automatic, people may not reliably notice their own triggers, which limits how much a self-rated risk questionnaire can capture.

cbi-9.title: 50 years of rational‐emotive and cognitive‐behavioral therapy: A systematic review and meta‐analysis
cbi-9.authors: Daniel David, Carmen Coteț, Silviu Andrei Matu, et al.
cbi-9.takeaway: A 50-year meta-analysis of rational-emotive and cognitive-behavioral therapy found medium effects on both distress and irrational beliefs, supporting the practice of disputing risky thoughts.

cbi-9.title: Do we need to challenge thoughts in cognitive behavior therapy?
cbi-9.takeaway: This review found little evidence that specifically challenging thoughts is what produces improvement in CBT.

cbi-9.title: A component analysis of cognitive-behavioral treatment for depression
cbi-9.authors: Neil S. Jacobson, Keith Stephen Dobson, Paula A. Truax, et al.
cbi-9.venue: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology
cbi-9.takeaway: In this classic component study for depression, behavioral activation alone did as well as full cognitive therapy, including at changing negative thinking.

cbi-10.title: Communication skills training, communication skills training with family and cognitive behavioral mood management training for alcoholics
cbi-10.authors: Peter M. Monti, David B. Abrams, Jody A. Binkoff, et al.
cbi-10.takeaway: Monti's trial found that skill shown in role plays of drinking situations was closely tied to later outcomes, supporting practice and role-play rather than discussion alone.

cbi-10.title: Computer-Assisted Delivery of Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy for Addiction: A Randomized Trial of CBT4CBT
cbi-10.authors: Kathleen M. Carroll, Samuel A. Ball, Steve Martino, et al.
cbi-10.takeaway: In the CBT4CBT trial, completing practice assignments predicted better outcomes, consistent with rehearsing replacement chains.

cbi-10.title: Cognitive–behavioral treatment for alcohol dependence: a review of evidence for its hypothesized mechanisms of action
cbi-10.takeaway: CBT's benefits were not clearly explained by gains in coping skill, so practiced skill may be only part of why members improve.

cbi-11.title: Self-efficacy: Toward a unifying theory of behavioral change
cbi-11.takeaway: Bandura's self-efficacy theory holds that past mastery experiences are the strongest source of confidence, the logic behind looking back at times members stayed clean.

cbi-11.title: The role of self-efficacy in the treatment of substance use disorders
cbi-11.authors: Ronald M. Kadden, Mark D. Litt
cbi-11.takeaway: This review found that self-efficacy reliably predicts substance use outcomes and can be raised in treatment.

cbi-11.title: The duration and correlates of addiction and treatment careers
cbi-11.authors: Michael L. Dennis, Christy K. Scott, Rodney R. Funk, et al.
cbi-11.takeaway: A long-term study found addiction careers often last decades with several treatment episodes, so most members will have earlier clean stretches to learn from.

cbi-12.title: Changing network support for drinking: Initial findings from the Network Support Project
cbi-12.authors: Mark D. Litt, Ronald M. Kadden, Elise Kabela‐Cormier, et al.
cbi-12.venue: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology
cbi-12.takeaway: The Network Support trial showed that treatment can change who people spend time with, and that those network changes contributed to better drinking outcomes.

cbi-12.title: Network Support as a Prognostic Indicator of Drinking Outcomes: The COMBINE Study
cbi-12.authors: Richard Longabaugh, Philip W. Wirtz, William H. Zywiak, et al.
cbi-12.venue: Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs
cbi-12.takeaway: In the COMBINE study, support for drinking in a person's social network predicted drinking outcomes, and grew more predictive over time.

cbi-12.title: Motivational Interviewing and Decisional Balance: Contrasting Responses to Client Ambivalence
cbi-12.authors: William R. Miller, Gary S. Rose
cbi-12.takeaway: A balanced cost-benefit listing can strengthen reasons to stay with risky people if the member is ambivalent; drawing out reasons for change may be more effective.

cbi-13.title: Network Support as a Prognostic Indicator of Drinking Outcomes: The COMBINE Study
cbi-13.authors: Richard Longabaugh, Philip W. Wirtz, William H. Zywiak, et al.
cbi-13.venue: Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs
cbi-13.takeaway: Alcohol-specific support in a person's network predicted drinking outcomes, which backs rating each important person for how they affect use.

cbi-13.title: Rehabilitating criminal justice policy and practice
cbi-13.authors: D. A. Andrews, James L. Bonta
cbi-13.takeaway: Risk-Need-Responsivity research lists antisocial associates among the strongest predictors of reoffending, supporting a close look at who helps or blocks goals.

cbi-13.title: Social network variables in alcoholics anonymous: A literature review
cbi-13.authors: David R. Groh, Leonard A. Jason, Christopher B. Keys
cbi-13.takeaway: This review found that changes in social networks are one of the main ways mutual-help groups help, showing the value of relationship audits.

cbi-14.title: Determining the relative importance of the mechanisms of behavior change within Alcoholics Anonymous: a multiple mediator analysis
cbi-14.authors: John Francis Kelly, Bettina B. Hoeppner, Robert L. Stout, et al.
cbi-14.takeaway: In this analysis of how AA works, changes in social networks explained more of the benefit than spirituality, pointing to support people as a key ingredient.

cbi-14.title: Changing network support for drinking: Initial findings from the Network Support Project
cbi-14.authors: Mark D. Litt, Ronald M. Kadden, Elise Kabela‐Cormier, et al.
cbi-14.venue: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology
cbi-14.takeaway: Treatment that helped people add supportive, non-using contacts improved drinking outcomes.

cbi-14.title: Social Relationships and Mortality Risk: A Meta-analytic Review
cbi-14.authors: Julianne Holt‐Lunstad, Timothy B. Smith, J. Bradley Layton
cbi-14.takeaway: A large meta-analysis linked strong social relationships to lower mortality on a scale comparable to well-known health risks.

cbi-15.title: Decreased substance use following increases in alternative behaviors: A preliminary investigation
cbi-15.authors: Christopher J. Correia, Trisha A. Benson, Kate Bergmann Carey
cbi-15.takeaway: Increases in substance-free activities were followed by decreases in use, supporting the idea that new rewards can compete with using.

cbi-15.title: A systematic review of the effectiveness of the community reinforcement approach in alcohol, cocaine and opioid addiction
cbi-15.authors: Hendrik G. Roozen, Jiska J. Boulogne, Maurits W. van Tulder, et al.
cbi-15.takeaway: This review found good evidence for the Community Reinforcement Approach, which builds a rewarding sober life, strongest for alcohol and for cocaine when combined with incentives.

cbi-15.title: Exercise as treatment for alcohol use disorders: systematic review and meta-analysis
cbi-15.authors: Mats Å. Hallgren, Davy Vancampfort, Esther S. Giesen, et al.
cbi-15.takeaway: Exercise is a common healthy activity, but this meta-analysis found it improved fitness and mood without reducing drinking, so one activity alone may not change use.

cbi-16.title: Emotion Regulation: Current Status and Future Prospects
cbi-16.takeaway: Gross's model treats emotions as signals that can be regulated at several points, matching the session's 'emotions are information' framing.

cbi-16.title: Deficits in emotion-regulation skills predict alcohol use during and after cognitive–behavioral therapy for alcohol dependence
cbi-16.authors: Matthias Berking, Matthias Margraf, David Daniel Ebert, et al.
cbi-16.venue: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology
cbi-16.takeaway: In alcohol-dependent patients, weak emotion-regulation skills, especially tolerating negative feelings, predicted drinking during and after CBT.

cbi-16.title: Addiction Motivation Reformulated: An Affective Processing Model of Negative Reinforcement
cbi-16.authors: Timothy B. Baker, Megan E. Piper, Danielle E. McCarthy, et al.
cbi-16.takeaway: Baker's negative-reinforcement model explains why bad feelings drive use: relief from distress becomes a powerful, partly automatic reason to use.

cbi-16.title: Emotion-regulation strategies across psychopathology: A meta-analytic review
cbi-16.authors: Amelia Aldao, Susan Nolen–Hoeksema, Susanne Schweizer
cbi-16.takeaway: Across disorders, rumination, avoidance, and suppression were more strongly tied to problems than helpful strategies were to wellbeing.

cbi-17.title: Deficits in emotion-regulation skills predict alcohol use during and after cognitive–behavioral therapy for alcohol dependence
cbi-17.authors: Matthias Berking, Matthias Margraf, David Daniel Ebert, et al.
cbi-17.venue: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology
cbi-17.takeaway: Emotion-regulation deficits, including recognizing and accepting feelings, predicted relapse, supporting a skill for noticing and naming emotions.

cbi-17.title: Emotion Regulation: Current Status and Future Prospects
cbi-17.takeaway: In Gross's extended model, identifying that an emotion needs regulating is the first stage, the step this session trains.

cbi-17.title: Emotion-regulation strategies across psychopathology: A meta-analytic review
cbi-17.authors: Amelia Aldao, Susan Nolen–Hoeksema, Susanne Schweizer
cbi-17.takeaway: The meta-analysis found adaptive strategies were only modestly linked to fewer symptoms, so naming feelings is necessary but not sufficient.

cbi-18.title: Emotion Regulation: Current Status and Future Prospects
cbi-18.takeaway: Reappraisal, changing how a situation is interpreted, is one of the best-studied emotion-regulation strategies and is what the Double Behavior Chain teaches.

cbi-18.title: 50 years of rational‐emotive and cognitive‐behavioral therapy: A systematic review and meta‐analysis
cbi-18.authors: Daniel David, Carmen Coteț, Silviu Andrei Matu, et al.
cbi-18.takeaway: REBT and CBT that target irrational beliefs produced medium effects on distress.

cbi-18.title: Do we need to challenge thoughts in cognitive behavior therapy?
cbi-18.takeaway: Evidence that cognitive change is what causes emotional improvement in CBT is thin.

cbi-19.title: Relaxation training for anxiety: a ten-years systematic review with meta-analysis
cbi-19.authors: Gian Mauro Manzoni, Francesco Pagnini, Gianluca Castelnuovo, et al.
cbi-19.takeaway: Relaxation training reliably lowers anxiety, supporting breathing and imagery as cool-down tools.

cbi-19.title: Does Venting Anger Feed or Extinguish the Flame? Catharsis, Rumination, Distraction, Anger, and Aggressive Responding
cbi-19.takeaway: Bushman found venting anger made people angrier and more aggressive than doing nothing; distraction worked better, supporting stepping away and counting.

cbi-19.title: Paradoxical effects of thought suppression: a meta-analysis of controlled studies
cbi-19.authors: Jonathan S. Abramowitz, David F. Tolin, Gordon P. Street
cbi-19.takeaway: If stepping away turns into pushing thoughts down, suppression research suggests the feeling may rebound, so the tools work best as short breaks, not avoidance.

cbi-20.title: Surfing the urge: Brief mindfulness-based intervention for college student smokers
cbi-20.takeaway: Urge surfing in this trial did not shrink urges, but people smoked less, which fits the session's message to ride cravings out rather than fight them.

cbi-20.title: Relative Efficacy of Mindfulness-Based Relapse Prevention, Standard Relapse Prevention, and Treatment as Usual for Substance Use Disorders
cbi-20.authors: Sarah W. Bowen, Katie A. Witkiewitz, Seema L. Clifasefi, et al.
cbi-20.takeaway: In a randomized trial, mindfulness-based relapse prevention led to less drug use and heavy drinking at 12 months than standard relapse prevention or usual care.

cbi-20.title: Association of Drug Cues and Craving With Drug Use and Relapse: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
cbi-20.takeaway: A large meta-analysis found that cues and cravings predict later use and relapse, confirming that urges are worth learning to handle.

cbi-20.title: Mindfulness-based Relapse Prevention for Substance Use Disorders: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
cbi-20.authors: Sean Grant, Benjamin Colaiaco, Aneesa Motala, et al.
cbi-20.takeaway: A systematic review found only small, low-confidence effects of mindfulness-based relapse prevention on craving and none on most other outcomes.

cbi-21.title: Deficits in emotion-regulation skills predict alcohol use during and after cognitive–behavioral therapy for alcohol dependence
cbi-21.authors: Matthias Berking, Matthias Margraf, David Daniel Ebert, et al.
cbi-21.venue: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology
cbi-21.takeaway: Better general emotion-regulation skills, especially tolerating distress, predicted less drinking after treatment, supporting a combined self-control skill.

cbi-21.title: Addiction Motivation Reformulated: An Affective Processing Model of Negative Reinforcement
cbi-21.authors: Timothy B. Baker, Megan E. Piper, Danielle E. McCarthy, et al.
cbi-21.takeaway: Because relief-seeking can run partly outside awareness, a structured self-control routine gives people a deliberate step before habit takes over.

cbi-21.title: Cognitive–behavioral treatment for alcohol dependence: a review of evidence for its hypothesized mechanisms of action
cbi-21.takeaway: Gains in coping skill have not clearly explained why CBT works, so a four-step skill may help less through the steps themselves than through practice and support.

cbi-22.title: Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy in the Treatment of Anger: A Meta-Analysis
cbi-22.takeaway: This meta-analysis of CBT for anger found that people who received it improved clearly more than untreated comparison groups, supporting a skills-based approach to anger.

cbi-22.title: Anger Management for Substance Use Disorder and Mental Health Clients: A Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy Manual
cbi-22.authors: Patrick M. Reilly, Michael S. Shopshire
cbi-22.takeaway: SAMHSA's anger manual uses the same building blocks: spotting cues early, a timeout plan, and cognitive restructuring, delivered to substance use clients.

cbi-22.title: A systematic review and meta-analysis on the effectiveness of CBT informed anger management
cbi-22.authors: Kevin Sammut Henwood, Shihning Chou, Kevin D. Browne
cbi-22.takeaway: CBT-informed anger management reduced reoffending, especially violent reoffending, and moderate-intensity programs did better than the most intensive ones.

cbi-22.title: Does batterers' treatment work? A meta-analytic review of domestic violence treatment
cbi-22.authors: Julia C. Babcock, Charles E. Green, Chet Robie
cbi-22.takeaway: For domestic violence, batterer programs (many anger-focused) had only small effects beyond the effect of arrest, so anger skills alone may not stop partner violence.

cbi-23.title: The role of stress in addiction relapse
cbi-23.takeaway: Sinha's review shows that stress and stress-induced craving increase relapse risk, supporting a stress check and coping plan.

cbi-23.title: Relaxation training for anxiety: a ten-years systematic review with meta-analysis
cbi-23.authors: Gian Mauro Manzoni, Francesco Pagnini, Gianluca Castelnuovo, et al.
cbi-23.takeaway: Relaxation training reduces anxiety consistently across studies.

cbi-23.title: Meta-analysis of Supplemental Treatment for Depressive and Anxiety Disorders in Patients Being Treated for Alcohol Dependence
cbi-23.authors: Jennifer Hobbs, Matt G. Kushner, Susanne S. Lee, et al.
cbi-23.takeaway: Adding treatment for co-occurring anxiety or depression to alcohol treatment modestly improved both psychiatric and drinking outcomes, so severe anxiety may need more than group skills.

cbi-23.title: Cognitive–behavioral treatment for alcohol dependence: a review of evidence for its hypothesized mechanisms of action
cbi-23.takeaway: Better coping skills have not clearly been shown to be how CBT reduces use.

cbi-24.title: Abstinence violation effect: Validation of an attributional construct with smoking cessation
cbi-24.authors: Susan J. Curry, G. Alan Marlatt, Judith R. Gordon
cbi-24.venue: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology
cbi-24.takeaway: This study supported the abstinence violation effect: blaming a slip on fixed personal failure made a return to full smoking more likely, which is why the session reframes setbacks.

cbi-24.title: Drinking trajectories following an initial lapse
cbi-24.authors: Katie A. Witkiewitz, Katherine E. Masyn
cbi-24.takeaway: After a first lapse, most people drank lightly and infrequently instead of spiraling, and coping behavior predicted who did better.

cbi-24.title: Moral Emotions and Moral Behavior
cbi-24.authors: June Price Tangney, Jeffrey B. Stuewig, Debra J. Mashek
cbi-24.takeaway: Tangney's review links guilt about a specific act to repair and shame about the whole self to hiding and defensiveness, supporting a focus on what to do next.

cbi-24.title: Relapse prevention for addictive behaviors
cbi-24.authors: Christian S. Hendershot, Katie A. Witkiewitz, William H. George, et al.
cbi-24.venue: Substance Abuse Treatment, Prevention, and Policy
cbi-24.takeaway: This review notes that because relapse prevention is usually folded into other treatments, individual parts like the abstinence-violation reframe have rarely been tested on their own.

cbi-25.title: Communication skills training, communication skills training with family and cognitive behavioral mood management training for alcoholics
cbi-25.authors: Peter M. Monti, David B. Abrams, Jody A. Binkoff, et al.
cbi-25.takeaway: Communication skills training improved outcomes for alcoholics in Monti's trial, and role-played social skill predicted results.

cbi-25.title: Theory-based active ingredients of effective treatments for substance use disorders
cbi-25.takeaway: Moos identifies social learning and building coping skills as active ingredients that effective substance use treatments share.

cbi-25.title: Cognitive–behavioral treatment for alcohol dependence: a review of evidence for its hypothesized mechanisms of action
cbi-25.takeaway: Skill-building treatments help, but studies have not shown that improved skills are the reason.

cbi-26.title: The Relative Effectiveness of Active Listening in Initial Interactions
cbi-26.authors: Harry Weger, Gina Castle Bell, Elizabeth M. Minei, et al.
cbi-26.takeaway: Active listening made people feel more understood than simple acknowledgments — and more than advice-giving did; the small effects were on secondary outcomes like satisfaction.

cbi-26.title: Is low therapist empathy toxic?
cbi-26.authors: Theresa B. Moyers, William R. Miller
cbi-26.takeaway: In addiction treatment, empathic listening by counselors was linked to better outcomes and confrontation to dropout and relapse, a reason to practice listening skills.

cbi-26.title: The alliance in adult psychotherapy: A meta-analytic synthesis
cbi-26.authors: Christoph Flückiger, A. C. Del Re, Bruce E. Wampold, et al.
cbi-26.takeaway: Across many psychotherapies, the quality of the working relationship reliably predicts outcome.

cbi-27.title: Moral Emotions and Moral Behavior
cbi-27.authors: June Price Tangney, Jeffrey B. Stuewig, Debra J. Mashek
cbi-27.takeaway: Tangney's review describes other-oriented empathy as the moral emotion that pulls people toward helping and away from harm.

cbi-27.title: Is low therapist empathy toxic?
cbi-27.authors: Theresa B. Moyers, William R. Miller
cbi-27.takeaway: Empathy research in addiction counseling shows how much accurately reading and reflecting another's feelings matters in relationships.

cbi-27.title: The Relative Effectiveness of Active Listening in Initial Interactions
cbi-27.authors: Harry Weger, Gina Castle Bell, Elizabeth M. Minei, et al.
cbi-27.takeaway: In this experiment, reflecting back what a partner said made people feel more understood — clearly more than advice-giving did — though effects on other outcomes were small, so reading others' feelings is helpful but not magic.

cbi-28.title: Communication skills training, communication skills training with family and cognitive behavioral mood management training for alcoholics
cbi-28.authors: Peter M. Monti, David B. Abrams, Jody A. Binkoff, et al.
cbi-28.takeaway: Skill in alcohol-specific role plays, such as turning down a drink, was strongly linked to outcomes.

cbi-28.title: Cue exposure with coping skills training and communication skills training for alcohol dependence: 6‐ and 12‐month outcomes
cbi-28.authors: Damaris J. Rohsenow, Peter M. Monti, Anthony V. Rubonis, et al.
cbi-28.takeaway: Communication skills training, including refusal practice, remained a promising part of alcohol treatment at 12 months.

cbi-28.title: Changing network support for drinking: Initial findings from the Network Support Project
cbi-28.authors: Mark D. Litt, Ronald M. Kadden, Elise Kabela‐Cormier, et al.
cbi-28.venue: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology
cbi-28.takeaway: Changing who one spends time with lowers how often refusal skills are needed in the first place.

cbi-28.title: Distinctions without a difference: Direct comparisons of psychotherapies for alcohol use disorders
cbi-28.authors: Zac E. Imel, Bruce E. Wampold, Scott D. Miller, et al.
cbi-28.takeaway: Direct comparisons of alcohol treatments found no reliable differences between approaches, which questions whether refusal-skill training is uniquely effective.

cbi-29.title: Assertiveness training: A forgotten evidence‐based treatment
cbi-29.authors: Brittany C. Speed, Brandon L. Goldstein, Marvin R. Goldfried
cbi-29.takeaway: This review argues assertiveness training is an effective but forgotten evidence-based treatment for several clinical problems.

cbi-29.title: Communication skills training, communication skills training with family and cognitive behavioral mood management training for alcoholics
cbi-29.authors: Peter M. Monti, David B. Abrams, Jody A. Binkoff, et al.
cbi-29.takeaway: Communication skills training, including expressing needs, helped alcohol-dependent patients.

cbi-29.title: Owning Your Emotions: Reactions to Expressions of Self- versus Other-Attributed Positive and Negative Emotions
cbi-29.authors: Amy M. Bippus, Stacy L. Young
cbi-29.takeaway: Listeners in this study did not react differently to 'I feel' versus 'you made me feel' wording for negative emotions, so phrasing may matter less than tone and timing.

cbi-30.title: Changing network support for drinking: Initial findings from the Network Support Project
cbi-30.authors: Mark D. Litt, Ronald M. Kadden, Elise Kabela‐Cormier, et al.
cbi-30.venue: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology
cbi-30.takeaway: The Network Support trial showed people can be coached to build and use supportive, non-using contacts, and that doing so improved drinking outcomes.

cbi-30.title: Determining the relative importance of the mechanisms of behavior change within Alcoholics Anonymous: a multiple mediator analysis
cbi-30.authors: John Francis Kelly, Bettina B. Hoeppner, Robert L. Stout, et al.
cbi-30.takeaway: Among the ways AA helps, changes in who people spend time with and how they are supported explained the most benefit.

cbi-30.title: Community reinforcement and family training: an effective option to engage treatment‐resistant substance‐abusing individuals in treatment
cbi-30.authors: Hendrik G. Roozen, Ranne de Waart, Petra J. A. van der Kroft
cbi-30.takeaway: CRAFT shows support works in both directions: coaching family members raised treatment entry far more than confrontational approaches.

cbi-31.title: Assertiveness training: A forgotten evidence‐based treatment
cbi-31.authors: Brittany C. Speed, Brandon L. Goldstein, Marvin R. Goldfried
cbi-31.takeaway: Assertiveness training has early research support for a range of problems and fits the session's calm, direct statement skill.

cbi-31.title: Owning Your Emotions: Reactions to Expressions of Self- versus Other-Attributed Positive and Negative Emotions
cbi-31.authors: Amy M. Bippus, Stacy L. Young
cbi-31.takeaway: Self-attributed 'I feel' statements were not received better than other-blaming ones for negative emotions in this study.

cbi-31.title: Communication skills training, communication skills training with family and cognitive behavioral mood management training for alcoholics
cbi-31.authors: Peter M. Monti, David B. Abrams, Jody A. Binkoff, et al.
cbi-31.takeaway: Communication skills training helped alcohol-dependent patients, though it bundled several skills together.

cbi-32.title: Expressed Emotion and Relapse of Psychopathology
cbi-32.takeaway: Hooley's review of expressed emotion links high criticism from family to relapse across disorders, showing why handling criticism calmly matters.

cbi-32.title: Assertiveness training: A forgotten evidence‐based treatment
cbi-32.authors: Brittany C. Speed, Brandon L. Goldstein, Marvin R. Goldfried
cbi-32.takeaway: Assertiveness training, which includes responding to criticism without aggression or giving in, has research support.

cbi-32.title: Communication skills training, communication skills training with family and cognitive behavioral mood management training for alcoholics
cbi-32.authors: Peter M. Monti, David B. Abrams, Jody A. Binkoff, et al.
cbi-32.takeaway: Role-practiced communication skills, including handling negative feedback, helped in alcohol treatment.

cbi-33.title: Rehabilitating criminal justice policy and practice
cbi-33.authors: D. A. Andrews, James L. Bonta
cbi-33.takeaway: The RNR model ranks antisocial associates among the biggest drivers of reoffending, backing the session's focus on avoiding trouble with others.

cbi-33.title: Network Support as a Prognostic Indicator of Drinking Outcomes: The COMBINE Study
cbi-33.authors: Richard Longabaugh, Philip W. Wirtz, William H. Zywiak, et al.
cbi-33.venue: Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs
cbi-33.takeaway: Network support for using predicted worse drinking outcomes over time.

cbi-33.title: The Effectiveness of Incarceration-Based Drug Treatment on Criminal Behavior: A Systematic Review
cbi-33.authors: Ojmarrh Mitchell, David B. Wilson, Doris Layton MacKenzie
cbi-33.venue: Campbell Systematic Reviews: Better Evidence for a Better World
cbi-33.takeaway: In prison-based programs, counseling cut reoffending but had little effect on drug use, so staying out of trouble and staying off substances may need separate plans.

cbi-34.title: Decreased substance use following increases in alternative behaviors: A preliminary investigation
cbi-34.authors: Christopher J. Correia, Trisha A. Benson, Kate Bergmann Carey
cbi-34.takeaway: In this study, people who increased substance-free activities then reduced their substance use, the core rationale for getting involved in a positive activity.

cbi-34.title: A systematic review of the effectiveness of the community reinforcement approach in alcohol, cocaine and opioid addiction
cbi-34.authors: Hendrik G. Roozen, Jiska J. Boulogne, Maurits W. van Tulder, et al.
cbi-34.takeaway: The Community Reinforcement Approach, which deliberately builds positive activities and relationships, has good evidence, especially for alcohol.

cbi-34.title: Exercise as treatment for alcohol use disorders: systematic review and meta-analysis
cbi-34.authors: Mats Å. Hallgren, Davy Vancampfort, Esther S. Giesen, et al.
cbi-34.takeaway: Exercise, a common positive activity, did not reduce drinking in this meta-analysis even though it helped depression and fitness, so one activity is rarely enough by itself.

cbi-35.title: Contingency management for treatment of substance use disorders: a meta‐analysis
cbi-35.authors: Michael L. Prendergast, Deborah Podus, John W. Finney, et al.
cbi-35.takeaway: Contingency management, which rewards sobriety with tangible incentives, was among the most effective treatments in this meta-analysis, supporting healthy rewards for wins.

cbi-35.title: Decreased substance use following increases in alternative behaviors: A preliminary investigation
cbi-35.authors: Christopher J. Correia, Trisha A. Benson, Kate Bergmann Carey
cbi-35.takeaway: When members' rewarding substance-free activities increased, their substance use went down, so a healthy celebration can be part of the same shift.

cbi-35.title: Theory-based active ingredients of effective treatments for substance use disorders
cbi-35.takeaway: Moos lists alternative rewards as one of the shared ingredients of effective substance treatment.

cbi-36.title: Problem solving and behavior modification
cbi-36.authors: Thomas J. D’Zurilla, Marvin R. Goldfried
cbi-36.takeaway: D'Zurilla and Goldfried's founding paper framed problem solving as a teachable sequence of steps, the model this module is built on, including slowing down before reacting.

cbi-36.title: The efficacy of problem solving therapy in reducing mental and physical health problems: A meta-analysis
cbi-36.authors: John M. Malouff, Einar Thorsteinsson, Nicola S. Schutte
cbi-36.takeaway: A meta-analysis found problem-solving therapy reduced mental and physical health problems compared with control conditions.

cbi-36.title: Problem-solving therapy for adult depression: An updated meta-analysis
cbi-36.authors: Pim J. Cuijpers, Leonore M. de Wit, Annet M. Kleiboer, et al.
cbi-36.takeaway: In depression trials, problem-solving therapy helped, but the effects were small, no larger than other therapies, and partly inflated by studies run by the method's own advocates.

cbi-37.title: Problem solving and behavior modification
cbi-37.authors: Thomas J. D’Zurilla, Marvin R. Goldfried
cbi-37.takeaway: In the classic model, defining the problem in concrete, factual terms and naming a goal comes first, because a vague problem cannot be solved.

cbi-37.title: Building a practically useful theory of goal setting and task motivation: A 35-year odyssey
cbi-37.authors: Edwin A. Locke, Gary P. Latham
cbi-37.takeaway: Goal-setting research shows that specific goals focus effort better than general ones, which supports writing a precise goal for each problem.

cbi-37.title: Problem-solving therapy for adult depression: An updated meta-analysis
cbi-37.authors: Pim J. Cuijpers, Leonore M. de Wit, Annet M. Kleiboer, et al.
cbi-37.takeaway: The meta-analysis found problem-solving therapy was not better than other treatments, so the step-by-step format is one good option rather than a uniquely powerful one.

cbi-38.title: Problem solving and behavior modification
cbi-38.authors: Thomas J. D’Zurilla, Marvin R. Goldfried
cbi-38.takeaway: The original model separates generating many alternatives from judging them, the same 'brainstorm first, weigh later' rule the session uses.

cbi-38.title: Problem-solving therapy for depression: A meta-analysis
cbi-38.authors: Alissa C. Bell, Thomas J. D’Zurilla
cbi-38.takeaway: In this meta-analysis for depression, problem-solving therapy worked better when it trained all the steps, including generating and evaluating options, than when it skipped some.

cbi-38.title: Problem-solving therapy for adult depression: An updated meta-analysis
cbi-38.authors: Pim J. Cuijpers, Leonore M. de Wit, Annet M. Kleiboer, et al.
cbi-38.takeaway: Problem-solving therapy's advantage shrank in better-controlled studies, a reminder that listing options helps but is not a cure-all.

cbi-39.title: Implementation Intentions and Goal Achievement: A Meta‐analysis of Effects and Processes
cbi-39.takeaway: Meta-analysis of implementation intentions shows that deciding exactly when, where, and how to act makes people much more likely to follow through, the core of a what/when/where/how plan.

cbi-39.title: Problem solving and behavior modification
cbi-39.authors: Thomas J. D’Zurilla, Marvin R. Goldfried
cbi-39.takeaway: Carrying out the chosen solution and then checking how it worked is the final step of the classic problem-solving model.

cbi-39.title: Goals Gone Wild: The Systematic Side Effects of Overprescribing Goal Setting
cbi-39.authors: Lisa D. Ordóñez, Maurice E. Schweitzer, Adam D. Galinsky, Max H. Bazerman
cbi-39.takeaway: Rigid or overly narrow targets can backfire by blinding people to other risks, so plans should be reviewed and adjusted rather than followed at any cost.

cbi-40.title: The efficacy of problem solving therapy in reducing mental and physical health problems: A meta-analysis
cbi-40.authors: John M. Malouff, Einar Thorsteinsson, Nicola S. Schutte
cbi-40.takeaway: Across many trials, structured problem-solving training reduced a range of health problems, supporting practice on members' real problems.

cbi-40.title: Problem-solving therapy for depression: A meta-analysis
cbi-40.authors: Alissa C. Bell, Thomas J. D’Zurilla
cbi-40.takeaway: Training all problem-solving steps together, as this wrap-up session does, produced the strongest effects.

cbi-40.title: Problem-solving therapy for adult depression: An updated meta-analysis
cbi-40.authors: Pim J. Cuijpers, Leonore M. de Wit, Annet M. Kleiboer, et al.
cbi-40.takeaway: The most recent meta-analysis judged problem-solving therapy effective but modest, about the same as other psychological treatments.

cbi-41.title: Relapse prevention for addictive behaviors
cbi-41.authors: Christian S. Hendershot, Katie A. Witkiewitz, William H. George, et al.
cbi-41.venue: Substance Abuse Treatment, Prevention, and Policy
cbi-41.takeaway: This review of relapse prevention supports mapping a person's own past and present risk factors and triggers as the base of a written plan.

cbi-41.title: Rehabilitating criminal justice policy and practice
cbi-41.authors: D. A. Andrews, James L. Bonta
cbi-41.takeaway: The Risk-Need-Responsivity model backs focusing a plan on each person's specific risk factors rather than a one-size-fits-all list.

cbi-41.title: Relapse Prevention for Alcohol and Drug Problems: That Was Zen, This Is Tao
cbi-41.authors: Katie A. Witkiewitz, G. Alan Marlatt
cbi-41.takeaway: Witkiewitz and Marlatt argue relapse is dynamic, with small changes sometimes causing sudden setbacks, so no written risk map can fully predict when danger will rise.

cbi-42.title: Relapse Prevention for Alcohol and Drug Problems: That Was Zen, This Is Tao
cbi-42.authors: Katie A. Witkiewitz, G. Alan Marlatt
cbi-42.takeaway: The updated relapse model pairs each high-risk situation with both thinking and behavioral coping responses, as the session's chains do.

cbi-42.title: Efficacy of relapse prevention: A meta-analytic review
cbi-42.authors: Jennifer E. Irvin, Clint A. Bowers, Michael E. Dunn, et al.
cbi-42.venue: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology
cbi-42.takeaway: A meta-analysis of 26 studies found relapse prevention generally effective, especially for alcohol and mixed substance problems.

cbi-42.title: Cognitive–behavioral treatment for alcohol dependence: a review of evidence for its hypothesized mechanisms of action
cbi-42.takeaway: Research has not shown that matching coping skills to situations is the reason CBT works, so the value may lie partly in the structure and support around the exercise.

cbi-43.title: Decreased substance use following increases in alternative behaviors: A preliminary investigation
cbi-43.authors: Christopher J. Correia, Trisha A. Benson, Kate Bergmann Carey
cbi-43.takeaway: In this study, increases in substance-free activities were followed by decreases in substance use, supporting planned replacements for risky free time.

cbi-43.title: Theory-based active ingredients of effective treatments for substance use disorders
cbi-43.takeaway: Moos identifies building alternative rewards and structured, goal-directed activity as ingredients shared by effective treatments.

cbi-43.title: A systematic review of the effectiveness of the community reinforcement approach in alcohol, cocaine and opioid addiction
cbi-43.authors: Hendrik G. Roozen, Jiska J. Boulogne, Maurits W. van Tulder, et al.
cbi-43.takeaway: The Community Reinforcement Approach, which rebuilds a rewarding sober lifestyle, had good evidence in this review, strongest for alcohol and for cocaine with added incentives.

cbi-43.title: Exercise as treatment for alcohol use disorders: systematic review and meta-analysis
cbi-43.authors: Mats Å. Hallgren, Davy Vancampfort, Esther S. Giesen, et al.
cbi-43.takeaway: Even a healthy replacement may not change use by itself: exercise improved mood and fitness but did not reduce drinking in this meta-analysis.

cbi-44.title: A simple scale of Gorski's warning signs for relapse
cbi-44.authors: William R. Miller, R. J. Harris
cbi-44.takeaway: A short scale of Gorski's relapse warning signs predicted later slips and relapses, supporting the session's work on spotting warning signs early.

cbi-44.title: Continuing care research: What we have learned and where we are going
cbi-44.takeaway: McKay's review shows that continuing care after the main program can help maintain gains, the logic behind planning to keep skills going after group.

cbi-44.title: How effective is continuing care for substance use disorders? A meta-analytic review
cbi-44.authors: Janet C. Blodgett, Natalya C. Maisel, Ingrid L. Fuh, et al.
cbi-44.takeaway: This meta-analysis found continuing care helped, but the average effect was small and varied a lot across studies.

cbi-45.title: Drinking trajectories following an initial lapse
cbi-45.authors: Katie A. Witkiewitz, Katherine E. Masyn
cbi-45.takeaway: After a first lapse, most people drank lightly and infrequently instead of returning to heavy use, and coping behavior predicted who recovered, which supports a bounce-back skill.

cbi-45.title: Abstinence violation effect: Validation of an attributional construct with smoking cessation
cbi-45.authors: Susan J. Curry, G. Alan Marlatt, Judith R. Gordon
cbi-45.venue: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology
cbi-45.takeaway: This study supported the abstinence violation effect: treating a slip as proof of personal failure made a full relapse more likely.

cbi-45.title: Profiles of recovery from alcohol use disorder at three years following treatment: can the definition of recovery be extended to include high functioning heavy drinkers?
cbi-45.authors: Katie A. Witkiewitz, Adam D. Wilson, Matthew Ryan Pearson, et al.
cbi-45.takeaway: Three years after treatment, some people who still drank heavily at times functioned as well as abstainers, which questions treating every return to use as total failure.

cbi-46.title: Implementation Intentions and Goal Achievement: A Meta‐analysis of Effects and Processes
cbi-46.takeaway: Rehearsing concrete if-then plans makes it more likely they will be carried out when the moment arrives.

cbi-46.title: Communication skills training, communication skills training with family and cognitive behavioral mood management training for alcoholics
cbi-46.authors: Peter M. Monti, David B. Abrams, Jody A. Binkoff, et al.
cbi-46.takeaway: In Monti's trial, how well patients handled role-played risky situations predicted their later outcomes, supporting rehearsal before presenting the plan.

cbi-46.title: Computer-Assisted Delivery of Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy for Addiction: A Randomized Trial of CBT4CBT
cbi-46.authors: Kathleen M. Carroll, Samuel A. Ball, Steve Martino, et al.
cbi-46.takeaway: In the CBT4CBT trial, completing practice assignments was tied to better results, consistent with finishing and checking the plan carefully.

cbi-46.title: A meta-analysis of outcome studies comparing bona fide psychotherapies: Empiricially, "all must have prizes."
cbi-46.authors: Bruce E. Wampold, Gregory W. Mondin, Marcia Moody, et al.
cbi-46.takeaway: Wampold's 'dodo bird' meta-analysis found genuine psychotherapies produce roughly equal results, suggesting shared factors like a good relationship and practice matter more than any one technique.

cbi-47.title: Self-efficacy: Toward a unifying theory of behavioral change
cbi-47.takeaway: Bandura's theory says confidence grows most from successful performance and from watching peers succeed, both of which happen when members present and role-play their plans.

cbi-47.title: Treating Drug Abuse and Addiction in the Criminal Justice System
cbi-47.authors: Redonna K. Chandler, Bennett W. Fletcher, Nora D. Volkow
cbi-47.takeaway: NIDA leaders argue that treatment in the justice system works best when care continues after release, so a finished plan should connect to community supports.

cbi-47.title: The Effectiveness of Incarceration-Based Drug Treatment on Criminal Behavior: A Systematic Review
cbi-47.authors: Ojmarrh Mitchell, David B. Wilson, Doris Layton MacKenzie
cbi-47.venue: Campbell Systematic Reviews: Better Evidence for a Better World
cbi-47.takeaway: In prison-based programs, counseling reduced reoffending but had little effect on drug use, a sober reminder that finishing a program does not by itself change use.

cbi-47.title: TIP 44: Substance Abuse Treatment for Adults in the Criminal Justice System
cbi-47.authors: Center for Substance Abuse Treatment (SAMHSA); consensus panel co-chairs Roger H. Peters, Harry K. Wexler
cbi-47.takeaway: SAMHSA's criminal-justice TIP stresses planning for the transition back to the community and linking people to continuing services, the purpose of a finished Success Plan.

lib-1.title: DSM-5 Criteria for Substance Use Disorders: Recommendations and Rationale
lib-1.authors: Deborah S. Hasin, Charles P. O’Brien, Marc Auriacombe, et al.
lib-1.takeaway: This paper explains the DSM-5 criteria for substance use disorder, including merging abuse and dependence and rating severity, which grounds the session's terms and self-rating.

lib-1.title: AUDIT: The Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test. Guidelines for Use in Primary Health Care (2nd ed.)
lib-1.takeaway: WHO's AUDIT manual shows that a short, structured questionnaire can identify hazardous and harmful drinking, the same idea as a self-assessment.

lib-1.title: Drug Dependence, a Chronic Medical Illness: Implications for Treatment, Insurance, and Outcomes Evaluation
lib-1.authors: A. Thomas McLellan, David C. Lewis, Charles P. O’Brien, et al.
lib-1.takeaway: McLellan and colleagues found that relapse and treatment adherence in drug dependence look similar to other chronic illnesses like diabetes and hypertension.

lib-1.title: Prevalence and pathways of recovery from drug and alcohol problems in the United States population: Implications for practice, research, and policy
lib-1.authors: John Francis Kelly, Brandon G. Bergman, Bettina B. Hoeppner, et al.
lib-1.takeaway: A national survey found tens of millions of Americans have resolved an alcohol or drug problem by many routes, a large share without formal treatment, which complicates the picture of addiction as a lifelong disease.

lib-2.title: Loss of Dopamine Transporters in Methamphetamine Abusers Recovers with Protracted Abstinence
lib-2.authors: Nora D. Volkow, Linda L. Chang, Gene‐Jack Wang, et al.
lib-2.takeaway: Brain scans showed dopamine transporters in people who used methamphetamine recovered with long abstinence, supporting the session's point that the brain heals over time.

lib-2.title: Neurobiologic Advances from the Brain Disease Model of Addiction
lib-2.authors: Nora D. Volkow, George F. Koob, A. Thomas McLellan
lib-2.takeaway: Volkow and colleagues summarize how repeated drug use changes reward, stress, and self-control circuits, the science behind the drug-class tour.

lib-2.title: The brain disease model of addiction: is it supported by the evidence and has it delivered on its promises?
lib-2.authors: Wayne Hall, Adrian Carter, Cynthia Forlini
lib-2.takeaway: Hall and colleagues argue the brain-disease account is less supported by evidence than claimed and has not produced better treatments.

lib-2.title: Brain Change in Addiction as Learning, Not Disease
lib-2.takeaway: Lewis argues the same brain changes are better understood as deep learning, like any strong habit, than as disease.

lib-3.title: Meta‐analysis of cue‐reactivity in addiction research
lib-3.authors: Brian Lee Carter, Stephen T. Tiffany
lib-3.takeaway: This meta-analysis found drug cues reliably trigger craving and body reactions, the trigger-to-craving link the session teaches.

lib-3.title: Association of Drug Cues and Craving With Drug Use and Relapse: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
lib-3.takeaway: A large meta-analysis found that cue reactivity and craving predict later drug use and relapse, supporting the session's focus on breaking the chain early.

lib-3.title: A cognitive model of drug urges and drug-use behavior: Role of automatic and nonautomatic processes
lib-3.takeaway: Tiffany argues much use is automatic and can happen without a strong craving, so waiting for a craving as the warning sign can miss lapses.

lib-3.title: Applying extinction research and theory to cue‐exposure addiction treatments
lib-3.authors: Cynthia A. Conklin, Stephen T. Tiffany
lib-3.takeaway: Cue-exposure treatments often fail because extinction learned in one setting does not carry over, which limits how far trigger training generalizes.

lib-4.title: A simple scale of Gorski's warning signs for relapse
lib-4.authors: William R. Miller, R. J. Harris
lib-4.takeaway: A scale of Gorski's warning signs predicted later slips and relapses, backing the session's focus on personal warning signs.

lib-4.title: Relapse Prevention for Alcohol and Drug Problems: That Was Zen, This Is Tao
lib-4.authors: Katie A. Witkiewitz, G. Alan Marlatt
lib-4.takeaway: Witkiewitz and Marlatt describe relapse as a process built from many interacting factors, close to the session's idea that relapse is a string of small choices.

lib-4.title: Drinking trajectories following an initial lapse
lib-4.authors: Katie A. Witkiewitz, Katherine E. Masyn
lib-4.takeaway: Most first lapses did not lead to heavy use, so relapse is less of a predictable downhill chain than the session's framing suggests.

lib-4.title: A quantitative review of the ubiquitous relapse curve
lib-4.authors: Ari P. Kirshenbaum, Darlene M. Olsen, Warren Kurt Bickel
lib-4.takeaway: Across studies, relapse curves look similar for different drugs, with most returns to use happening early after treatment.

lib-5.title: Alcohol use and burden for 195 countries and territories, 1990–2016: a systematic analysis for the Global Burden of Disease Study 2016
lib-5.authors: GBD 2016 Alcohol Collaborators (Griswold, Fullman, Hawley, et al.)
lib-5.takeaway: The Global Burden of Disease analysis found the level of drinking that minimizes health loss is zero, supporting 'legal isn't safe'.

lib-5.title: Mortality Following Inpatient Addictions Treatment: Role of Tobacco Use in a Community-Based Cohort
lib-5.authors: Richard D. Hurt, Kenneth P. Offord, Ivana T. Croghan, et al.
lib-5.takeaway: Among people treated for alcohol or drug dependence, more later deaths were caused by tobacco than by alcohol, a strong reason to address smoking too.

lib-5.title: A Meta-Analysis of Smoking Cessation Interventions With Individuals in Substance Abuse Treatment or Recovery
lib-5.authors: Judith J. Prochaska, Kevin Delucchi, Sharon Martinelli Hall
lib-5.venue: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology
lib-5.takeaway: Smoking-cessation help during addiction treatment was linked to a 25% higher chance of long-term sobriety, refuting the fear that quitting both is too much.

lib-5.title: Profiles of recovery from alcohol use disorder at three years following treatment: can the definition of recovery be extended to include high functioning heavy drinkers?
lib-5.authors: Katie A. Witkiewitz, Adam D. Wilson, Matthew Ryan Pearson, et al.
lib-5.takeaway: Some people who drank heavily now and then after treatment functioned as well as abstainers, which questions abstinence as the only measure of recovery.

lib-6.title: Spirituality in Recovery: A Lagged Mediational Analysis of Alcoholics Anonymous’ Principal Theoretical Mechanism of Behavior Change
lib-6.authors: John Francis Kelly, Robert L. Stout, Molly Magill, et al.
lib-6.takeaway: This analysis found that AA helps people drink less partly by increasing spiritual practices, supporting a role for spirituality.

lib-6.title: Alcoholics Anonymous Effectiveness: Faith Meets Science
lib-6.takeaway: Kaskutas reviews the evidence that AA works, finding it strong on some scientific criteria and mixed on others.

lib-6.title: Determining the relative importance of the mechanisms of behavior change within Alcoholics Anonymous: a multiple mediator analysis
lib-6.authors: John Francis Kelly, Bettina B. Hoeppner, Robert L. Stout, et al.
lib-6.takeaway: In a comparison of AA's mechanisms, social changes mattered more than spirituality, suggesting spirituality is one route among several.

lib-6.title: Matching Alcoholism Treatments to Client Heterogeneity: Project MATCH posttreatment drinking outcomes
lib-6.takeaway: In Project MATCH, a spiritually based Twelve Step Facilitation therapy did about as well as CBT and motivational therapy, so a spiritual approach is one effective option among several.

lib-7.title: Understanding Acute Alcohol Effects on Sexual Behavior
lib-7.authors: William H. George, Susan A. Stoner
lib-7.takeaway: George and Stoner review lab evidence that alcohol raises sexual risk-taking, mostly by narrowing attention to the moment (alcohol myopia).

lib-7.title: Chemsex behaviours among men who have sex with men: A systematic review of the literature
lib-7.authors: Steven Maxwell, Maryam Shahmanesh, Mitzy Gafos
lib-7.takeaway: This review of 'chemsex' links drugs used for sex with sexual risk and harms, supporting the session's point that sex can become a trigger.

lib-7.title: Harm reduction: Come as you are
lib-7.takeaway: Marlatt's harm-reduction view meets people where they are, which in practice means teaching safer-sex and safer-use steps alongside the goal of not mixing sex and drugs.

lib-8.title: Chronic Stress, Drug Use, and Vulnerability to Addiction
lib-8.venue: Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences
lib-8.takeaway: Sinha's review connects chronic stress to drug use and relapse vulnerability, the reason stress gets its own session.

lib-8.title: Addiction Motivation Reformulated: An Affective Processing Model of Negative Reinforcement
lib-8.authors: Timothy B. Baker, Megan E. Piper, Danielle E. McCarthy, et al.
lib-8.takeaway: Baker's model explains how using to escape bad feelings becomes a strong, partly automatic driver of use.

lib-8.title: Emotion-regulation strategies across psychopathology: A meta-analytic review
lib-8.authors: Amelia Aldao, Susan Nolen–Hoeksema, Susanne Schweizer
lib-8.takeaway: Across disorders, how people respond to stress, especially avoidance and rumination, was tied to psychological problems.

lib-8.title: Cognitive–behavioral treatment for alcohol dependence: a review of evidence for its hypothesized mechanisms of action
lib-8.takeaway: Better coping was not shown to explain why CBT helps, so stress lessons may help less through skills than expected.

lib-9.title: Relaxation training for anxiety: a ten-years systematic review with meta-analysis
lib-9.authors: Gian Mauro Manzoni, Francesco Pagnini, Gianluca Castelnuovo, et al.
lib-9.takeaway: This meta-analysis found relaxation training reliably reduced anxiety, supporting deliberate relaxation practice.

lib-9.title: Mindfulness-based interventions for psychiatric disorders: A systematic review and meta-analysis
lib-9.authors: Simon Benjamin Goldberg, Raymond P. Tucker, Preston A. Greene, et al.
lib-9.takeaway: Mindfulness-based programs beat no treatment and matched other evidence-based treatments, with evidence for addictive disorders.

lib-9.title: Social Relationships and Mortality Risk: A Meta-analytic Review
lib-9.authors: Julianne Holt‐Lunstad, Timothy B. Smith, J. Bradley Layton
lib-9.takeaway: Strong social ties were linked to longer life, backing the session's advice to lean on the right people.

lib-9.title: Cognitive–behavioral treatment for alcohol dependence: a review of evidence for its hypothesized mechanisms of action
lib-9.takeaway: CBT's benefits were not explained by improved coping skills, a caution for expecting stress skills alone to change use.

lib-10.title: Meta-analysis of Supplemental Treatment for Depressive and Anxiety Disorders in Patients Being Treated for Alcohol Dependence
lib-10.authors: Jennifer Hobbs, Matt G. Kushner, Susanne S. Lee, et al.
lib-10.takeaway: Adding treatment for depression or anxiety to alcohol treatment improved both mood and drinking modestly, supporting telling sadness from depression and getting help.

lib-10.title: Moral Emotions and Moral Behavior
lib-10.authors: June Price Tangney, Jeffrey B. Stuewig, Debra J. Mashek
lib-10.takeaway: Tangney's review separates guilt (about an act, which motivates repair) from shame (about the self, linked to hiding), useful for the session's work on guilt.

lib-10.title: Efficacy of psychotherapeutic interventions to promote forgiveness: A meta-analysis
lib-10.authors: Nathaniel G. Wade, William T. Hoyt, Julia E. M. Kidwell, et al.
lib-10.venue: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology
lib-10.takeaway: A meta-analysis of therapy programs designed to promote forgiveness found they helped people resolve past hurts more than no treatment or other therapies.

lib-10.title: The Dark Side of Forgiveness: The Tendency to Forgive Predicts Continued Psychological and Physical Aggression in Marriage
lib-10.takeaway: McNulty found that in marriages, forgiving a partner who kept being aggressive predicted continued aggression, so forgiveness is not always safe advice.

lib-11.title: Anger Management for Substance Use Disorder and Mental Health Clients: A Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy Manual
lib-11.authors: Patrick M. Reilly, Michael S. Shopshire
lib-11.takeaway: SAMHSA's anger manual for substance use clients teaches the same core steps: noticing body cues, a timeout, and calm assertive expression.

lib-11.title: Does Venting Anger Feed or Extinguish the Flame? Catharsis, Rumination, Distraction, Anger, and Aggressive Responding
lib-11.takeaway: Venting anger made people angrier and more aggressive than doing nothing, supporting the session's drop of bad anger habits.

lib-11.title: Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy in the Treatment of Anger: A Meta-Analysis
lib-11.takeaway: CBT for anger produced clear improvement over untreated groups in this meta-analysis.

lib-11.title: Owning Your Emotions: Reactions to Expressions of Self- versus Other-Attributed Positive and Negative Emotions
lib-11.authors: Amy M. Bippus, Stacy L. Young
lib-11.takeaway: Listeners did not react better to 'I feel' statements than to blaming ones for negative emotions, so wording alone may not calm conflicts.

lib-12.title: Efficacy of relapse prevention: A meta-analytic review
lib-12.authors: Jennifer E. Irvin, Clint A. Bowers, Michael E. Dunn, et al.
lib-12.venue: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology
lib-12.takeaway: This meta-analysis found relapse prevention generally effective, particularly for alcohol problems.

lib-12.title: Comparative cocaine abuse treatment strategies: Enhancing client retention and treatment exposure
lib-12.authors: Jeffrey A. Hoffman, Barry D. Caudill, Joseph J. Koman, et al.
lib-12.takeaway: In the early randomized trial behind Living in Balance, the enhanced programs — the intensive LIB program and enhanced standard group therapy alike — kept cocaine clients in treatment longer and for more sessions than standard group therapy alone.

lib-12.title: A meta-analysis of cognitive-behavioral therapy for alcohol or other drug use disorders: Treatment efficacy by contrast condition
lib-12.authors: Molly Magill, Lara A. Ray, Brian D. Kiluk, et al.
lib-12.venue: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology
lib-12.takeaway: This meta-analysis found CBT-based relapse work beats no or minimal treatment, but is not better than other active treatments, so the specific method may matter less than staying engaged.

lib-12.title: Living in Balance (Continuum of Evidence fact sheet)
lib-12.authors: Clearinghouse for Military Family Readiness, Penn State
lib-12.takeaway: The Penn State clearinghouse found no peer-reviewed evaluation of the current Living in Balance version, so the curriculum's evidence comes mostly from its parts and an early trial.

lib-13.title: Alcoholics Anonymous and other 12-step programs for alcohol use disorder
lib-13.authors: John Francis Kelly, Keith N. Humphreys, Marica Ferri
lib-13.takeaway: The 2020 Cochrane review found manualized AA/Twelve Step Facilitation led to more continuous abstinence than other established treatments such as CBT, and likely saves health costs.

lib-13.title: Estimating the Efficacy of Alcoholics Anonymous without Self‐Selection Bias: An Instrumental Variables Re‐Analysis of Randomized Clinical Trials
lib-13.authors: Keith N. Humphreys, Janet C. Blodgett, Todd H. Wagner
lib-13.takeaway: Using a method that removes self-selection bias, this study found that attending more AA meetings itself reduced drinking for most help-seekers.

lib-13.title: A longitudinal study of the comparative efficacy of Women for Sobriety, LifeRing, SMART Recovery, and 12-step groups for those with AUD
lib-13.authors: Sarah E. Zemore, Camillia K. Lui, Amy A. Mericle, et al.
lib-13.takeaway: In this longitudinal study, members of SMART Recovery, LifeRing, and Women for Sobriety did about as well as Twelve Step members, supporting the session's mention of secular alternatives.

lib-13.title: Alcoholics Anonymous and other 12-step programmes for alcohol dependence
lib-13.authors: Marica Ferri, Laura Amato, Marina Davoli
lib-13.takeaway: The earlier 2006 Cochrane review found no experimental studies that clearly proved AA or TSF effective, showing how much the evidence depends on study design.

lib-14.title: Alcoholics Anonymous and other 12-step programs for alcohol use disorder
lib-14.authors: John Francis Kelly, Keith N. Humphreys, Marica Ferri
lib-14.takeaway: The 2020 Cochrane review found manualized Twelve Step Facilitation at least as effective as other treatments such as CBT, and better for keeping people continuously abstinent.

lib-14.title: Spirituality in Recovery: A Lagged Mediational Analysis of Alcoholics Anonymous’ Principal Theoretical Mechanism of Behavior Change
lib-14.authors: John Francis Kelly, Robert L. Stout, Molly Magill, et al.
lib-14.takeaway: AA helped people drink less partly by increasing their spiritual practices, consistent with the spiritual principles behind the steps.

lib-14.title: Determining the relative importance of the mechanisms of behavior change within Alcoholics Anonymous: a multiple mediator analysis
lib-14.authors: John Francis Kelly, Bettina B. Hoeppner, Robert L. Stout, et al.
lib-14.takeaway: When several of AA's mechanisms were compared, social changes like new sober friends explained more benefit than spirituality, suggesting the fellowship matters as much as the steps themselves.

lib-14.title: Alcoholics Anonymous Effectiveness: Faith Meets Science
lib-14.takeaway: Kaskutas finds the case for AA strong on several scientific criteria for cause and effect, but mixed on whether facilitation programs themselves cause the benefit.

lib-17.title: Impact of Physical Exercise on Substance Use Disorders: A Meta-Analysis
lib-17.authors: Dongshi Wang, Yanqiu Wang, Yingying Wang, et al.
lib-17.takeaway: This meta-analysis found moderate and high-intensity aerobic and mind-body exercise improved abstinence and reduced withdrawal and depression symptoms in people with substance use disorders.

lib-17.title: The importance of nutrition in aiding recovery from substance use disorders: A review
lib-17.authors: Kendall D. Jeynes, Edward Leigh Gibson
lib-17.takeaway: This review describes how substance use damages nutrition and argues that improving diet can aid recovery, including mood and craving.

lib-17.title: Exercise as treatment for alcohol use disorders: systematic review and meta-analysis
lib-17.authors: Mats Å. Hallgren, Davy Vancampfort, Esther S. Giesen, et al.
lib-17.takeaway: For alcohol use disorder specifically, exercise did not reduce drinking, though it improved depression and fitness.

lib-18.title: Insomnia, alcoholism and relapse
lib-18.takeaway: Brower's review shows insomnia is common in early recovery from alcohol and is linked to relapse, supporting attention to sleep.

lib-18.title: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Chronic Insomnia: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
lib-18.authors: James McCracken Trauer, Mary Y. Qian, Joseph Doyle, et al.
lib-18.takeaway: CBT for insomnia produced clinically meaningful improvements in this meta-analysis, so the behavioral sleep tips in the session have strong backing.

lib-18.title: Mortality Following Inpatient Addictions Treatment: Role of Tobacco Use in a Community-Based Cohort
lib-18.authors: Richard D. Hurt, Kenneth P. Offord, Ivana T. Croghan, et al.
lib-18.takeaway: Many health problems ignored during use matter: in people treated for addiction, tobacco caused more later deaths than alcohol did.

lib-18.title: Cognitive-behavioral therapy for insomnia in alcohol dependent patients: A randomized controlled pilot trial
lib-18.authors: John Todd Arnedt, Deirdre A. Conroy, Roseanne Armitage, et al.
lib-18.takeaway: In a small trial with alcohol-dependent patients, CBT for insomnia improved sleep but did not change relapse rates, so better sleep may not by itself prevent relapse.

lib-19.title: Problem solving and behavior modification
lib-19.authors: Thomas J. D’Zurilla, Marvin R. Goldfried
lib-19.takeaway: D'Zurilla and Goldfried's model treats problem solving as a set of learnable steps, the basis of the session's six-step method.

lib-19.title: The efficacy of problem solving therapy in reducing mental and physical health problems: A meta-analysis
lib-19.authors: John M. Malouff, Einar Thorsteinsson, Nicola S. Schutte
lib-19.takeaway: Problem-solving therapy reduced mental and physical health problems across many studies.

lib-19.title: Problem-solving therapy for adult depression: An updated meta-analysis
lib-19.authors: Pim J. Cuijpers, Leonore M. de Wit, Annet M. Kleiboer, et al.
lib-19.takeaway: Problem-solving therapy's effects were small and no larger than other therapies, partly inflated by researcher allegiance.

lib-20.title: 50 years of rational‐emotive and cognitive‐behavioral therapy: A systematic review and meta‐analysis
lib-20.authors: Daniel David, Carmen Coteț, Silviu Andrei Matu, et al.
lib-20.takeaway: This 50-year meta-analysis found that REBT, the source of the 'beliefs, not events, drive stress' idea, had medium effects on distress and on irrational beliefs.

lib-20.title: Do we need to challenge thoughts in cognitive behavior therapy?
lib-20.takeaway: Longmore and Worrell found little evidence that disputing thoughts is the part of CBT that produces improvement.

lib-20.title: A component analysis of cognitive-behavioral treatment for depression
lib-20.authors: Neil S. Jacobson, Keith Stephen Dobson, Paula A. Truax, et al.
lib-20.venue: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology
lib-20.takeaway: In this component study, a behavior-only treatment improved depression and even negative thinking as much as full cognitive therapy, which questions whether beliefs must be disputed directly.

lib-21.title: Social Relationships and Mortality Risk: A Meta-analytic Review
lib-21.authors: Julianne Holt‐Lunstad, Timothy B. Smith, J. Bradley Layton
lib-21.takeaway: Strong social relationships were linked to lower mortality on a scale comparable to smoking, supporting the session's focus on real connection.

lib-21.title: Needs and subjective well-being around the world
lib-21.venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
lib-21.takeaway: In worldwide survey data, meeting different needs each predicted well-being largely on its own, regardless of whether 'lower' needs were met first, which questions a strict hierarchy of needs.

lib-21.title: Network Support as a Prognostic Indicator of Drinking Outcomes: The COMBINE Study
lib-21.authors: Richard Longabaugh, Philip W. Wirtz, William H. Zywiak, et al.
lib-21.venue: Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs
lib-21.takeaway: In COMBINE, a social network supportive of drinking predicted worse outcomes over time, showing why relationships shape recovery.

lib-21.title: Decreased substance use following increases in alternative behaviors: A preliminary investigation
lib-21.authors: Christopher J. Correia, Trisha A. Benson, Kate Bergmann Carey
lib-21.takeaway: Substance-free rewarding activities competed with use, matching the idea that using crowded out healthy needs.

lib-22.title: TIP 39: Substance Use Disorder Treatment and Family Therapy
lib-22.authors: Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration
lib-22.takeaway: SAMHSA's family therapy TIP explains how substance use shapes whole-family patterns and how to bring families into treatment.

lib-22.title: Behavioral couples therapy (BCT) for alcohol and drug use disorders: A meta-analysis
lib-22.authors: Mark B. Powers, Ellen Vedel, Paul M.G. Emmelkamp
lib-22.takeaway: Behavioral couples therapy did better than individual treatment for married or cohabiting people with alcohol or drug dependence.

lib-22.title: Community reinforcement and family training: an effective option to engage treatment‐resistant substance‐abusing individuals in treatment
